transcript: Ben Macintyre, thank you for joining us on the Lawfare podcast today. You created a sort of cottage industry by exploiting the lesser- known corners of intelligence warfare, both among the Allied forces in World War II and in the Cold War between the West and the Soviet Empire. And that means money, ideology, coercion, and ego. You may have written the first chronicle of an intelligence operation that was catalyzed by an acute case of erectile dysfunction. That's true, Michael. This is the first case of this type that I have come across. Tell me if you've ever come across this. I mean, that's what makes this story quite bizarre in some ways. Money, ideology, coercion, and ego. These are the easiest acronyms to use. It's a bit reductionist, as they say. In the case of this particular spy, a man named Vladimir Kuzichkin, he was a senior KGB officer operating in revolutionary and post-revolutionary Iran. So, he's in the hot cauldron of revolutionary politics. And money was never his motivation. He volunteered to spy for the British. He was a guy who didn't move. So, he literally walked into the British embassy in 1981 and said he wanted to spy for the West, he wanted to spy for MI6. His motivations were very different from the norm. Money never had a role. The ideology was there. He was very alienated from the Soviet regime and was fed up with the KGB. Coercion? Absolutely not . And ego? It really isn't a factor, because his weaknesses were, in many ways, far more pronounced than his ego. He suffered from erectile dysfunction, which sounds comical, but for him it was a nightmare. He was trying to save his marriage. The stress of being a KGB agent in intensely hostile circumstances in Iran was taking its toll on him. And he believed, like many Soviets, that the West had remedies that would cure him. Many Soviet citizens had a somewhat exaggerated belief in Western medicine, viewing it almost as a form of magic that would somehow cure anything. And he believed there were pills that would save his marriage, get his sex life back on track, and so he, you know, his deal was that he'd say, "I'm going to spy in the West for a year, and then I want to settle down in the West with my wife, and I want to start over. " So he had this kind of fantasy about what was going to happen. And of course, Viagra hadn't been invented yet at that time. There was no cure for it. But MI6 couldn't really say that. But there was very little they could do to help. So, time has been passing in this story from the very beginning. Now, before we get into the details of the operation, could you describe the scenario? Most Americans, when they think of revolutionary Iran, immediately think of the hostage crisis involving the American embassy. But his book, particularly in the initial chapters, presents a solid argument for why Iran was a key state, what historians would call non- aligned, in the Cold War. Why were MI6 and the CIA, on the one hand, and the KGB, on the other, so interested in a small state that, frankly, at this moment is nowhere near being a world power? Well, I would put that into perspective. I mean , there's a one- word answer to that question, and that's oil. Oil. Iran was a key state in the Cold War . We often forget this now, but the great powers were fighting over Iran 200 years ago. The Russians advancing from the north, imperial Britain trying to hold the line in Iran to defend India, the jewel of the empire. But this Great Game, as it was called, gave way to a similar dispute in the Cold War, but this time between the communist Soviet Union on one side and the capitalist West on the other, led by the United States. So, with the Shah in power in the 1970s, Iran was seen as a kind of buffer state against communism. He was completely aligned with the West. The Shah was the United States' favorite despot . He was autocratic. He was prepared to follow the American line and he was prepared to contain the Soviets. He maintained relations with the Soviets, but kept them at a distance. So what you really had was MI6 and the CIA coordinating with the Shah's brutal internal security service, SAVAK, an extremely formidable organization, partly trained by the CIA. And they were fundamentally anti-Soviet. The KGB was losing the espionage war, so to speak, in pre-revolutionary Iran. When the revolution happens, everything turns upside down. There is a hostage crisis. The Americans are effectively expelled from Iran. There were 50,000 Americans living in Iran before the revolution. Everyone is forced to leave. Diplomatic relations between the United States and Tehran are severed. The British maintain a small diplomatic representation in post-revolutionary Iran, but they are really, really small. And for the KGB, this is an opportunity. This is their chance to move into what was effectively a power vacuum . I mean, we often think of revolutions as overnight changes in societies, you know, that they somehow transform everything. This is not entirely true in Iran, because although the Ayatollah and his Islamic regime were on the rise and had seized power, many other groups were competing for influence and power in Iran. I mean, Kuzichkin, this character, this Vladimir Kuzichkin, his main function as a KGB officer was to coordinate with the Iranian Communist Party, the Tudeh Party.
